---
title: "Exercises — Turning chemistry into sequence"
---

Pen and paper. Try each one before opening the **Hint**, and the hint before the
**Solution** — the reasoning is the point, not the answer.

# Part 1 — Reading conversions

## E1. Read the methylation

A reference reads `ACGTCCGATCGA` (all three CpGs are at positions 2–3, 6–7 and 10–11). After
bisulfite and PCR, one molecule reads `ACGTTTGATCGA`. Which CpGs were methylated on that
molecule? Which of the Cs outside CpG did the data tell you about, and what did they say?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Compare each reference C with the read. C stays C only if it was protected.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The Cs at positions 2 and 10 stayed C: those two CpGs were methylated. The C at position 6 became
T, so that CpG was unmethylated. The C at position 5 (outside CpG) also became T, which is what
you expect for a non-CpG C in human DNA. All four reference Cs are informative; a T opposite a
reference T would not have been.
:::

## E2. How much can you trust a low number?

You add unmethylated lambda DNA to your sample. Lambda has 12,000 cytosines in the reads, and
108 of them read C. A promoter CpG in the sample is called 2% methylated. What is the
conversion rate, and what does it say about the 2%?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Failed conversion shows up as unmethylated C that reads C.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
108/12,000 = 0.9% read C, so the conversion rate is 99.1% and the false methylation rate is about 0.9%.
A call of 2% is only about twice that background, so it is weak evidence of methylation; you
would want replicates, higher depth, or a better conversion. Subtracting the background gives roughly
1.1% real methylation, but with such small numbers that subtraction is not reliable on its own.
:::

## E3. A trap: a SNP that looks like a conversion

At one position your reference has C and a sample has a C to T germline SNP. In bisulfite data
the position reads T. Why is this a problem, and how can the data on the other strand help?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Which strand's base is changed by bisulfite? What is on the opposite strand at this position?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Unmethylated C and a C to T SNP both give T, so the position looks unmethylated when it is
actually a different genotype. The opposite strand carries G at that position if the base was
C, and A if it was T. Bisulfite does not change G or A, so the opposite strand gives the true
genotype. A G there means the C was present and the T was conversion; an A means a SNP. Calling
variants from converted data needs both strands.
:::

# Part 2 — Choosing a chemistry

## E4. 5mC or 5hmC?

At one CpG in brain DNA, bisulfite reads 60% C and oxBS-seq reads 45% C. How much 5mC, 5hmC
and unmodified C is there? What does the TAB-seq number at this site have to be, if the data are consistent?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Which of the two reads C for both marks, and which for only one?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Bisulfite reads C for 5mC and 5hmC together: 60%. oxBS reads C for 5mC only: 45%. So 5mC is 45%,
5hmC is 60 minus 45, which is 15%, and the unmodified fraction is 40%. TAB-seq reads C for 5hmC
only, so it should be about 15%. The subtraction of two noisy percentages carries both errors, so
at low 5hmC the difference can be smaller than the noise.
:::

## E5. Picking between bisulfite and an enzymatic method

You have cell-free DNA from 2 ml of plasma, a few nanograms, and want methylation at base
resolution. List what bisulfite does to the material, why that matters at this input, and
which of the methods in the lecture you would choose.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Cell-free DNA is already about 170 bp long. What does a harsh treatment do to what is left?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Bisulfite is acidic and hot: it fragments DNA and damages part of it, so a good fraction of the
few nanograms cannot be amplified. EM-seq is the natural choice because the conversion is enzymatic,
with less loss. TAPS is also gentle and keeps the read four-letter. Either way, include the spike-ins. Which of the two to pick
is a matter of kit availability, input and whether you want 5hmC separated.
:::

## E6. Read a label or enrich it

You want to measure RNA synthesis in cultured cells over one hour with 4-thiouridine. Compare
(a) a T to C conversion readout with (b) biotinylating the labelled RNA and pulling it down.
Which problems does each have?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Think about what happens to RNA that is not labelled, and what bias a pull-down introduces.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
(a) Conversion reads the label per molecule and needs no pull-down, so old and new RNA come from
the same library and ratios are direct. It needs enough Ts and enough label for a mismatch to
show, and sequencing errors give a background, so a no-label control is required.
(b) Enrichment concentrates the new RNA and so works with little label, but captured and
unbound fractions are two libraries with different efficiencies, and RNA can stick non-specifically
to beads. A no-label pull-down shows how large that background is.
:::

# Part 3 — Positions

## E7. Where does the iCLIP read start?

A protein is crosslinked to nucleotide 100 of an RNA. Reverse transcription proceeds from the 3'
end towards the 5' end. Where does the cDNA end? Why is that a feature, and what do reads that
read through the site do to your peak?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Remember that the peptide left on the base is a physical obstacle for the enzyme.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Truncated cDNAs end at nucleotide 101 (one base 3' of the crosslink), so the first base of the
read is the nucleotide next to the crosslink. Because the reverse transcriptase stops there, each truncated
molecule marks the position, which is the signal. Reads that pass through carry the peptide
without stopping and add noise elsewhere; they do not move the peak. A size-matched input without
the antibody shows how much of the pattern comes from unrelated truncations.
:::

## E8. Reduced representation: cost and failure

You want methylation at CpG-rich regions across 96 samples. Whole-genome bisulfite at 30x costs
about 93 Gb per sample. Suppose that RRBS covers 2% of a 3.1 Gb genome at 20x. Estimate the sequencing per
sample and say what you lose. Then say what goes wrong in the first bases of the read.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Multiply genome size by the fraction covered and by the depth. For the first bases, what does
the restriction enzyme cut leave at every fragment end?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
3.1 Gb × 2% × 20 = about 1.2 Gb per sample, under 2% of the whole-genome cost, so 96 samples
need about 120 Gb in total. You lose everything outside the fragments that MspI produces in
the size window, which is largely CpGs outside islands and promoters. All fragments begin with
the same cut-site sequence, and after conversion the next bases are mostly T, so the first cycles
are low in diversity and the base calling (and cluster calling) suffers. Spike in PhiX or use a
library design that avoids the constant start.
:::

## E9. Pick the readout

For each question, choose conversion, antibody enrichment or native readout, and give the
property that decides: (a) fraction of 5mC at a single CpG in 5 ng of DNA; (b) regions enriched
for 5mC in about 1000 cells of DNA; (c) whether two methylations on the
same 20 kb molecule occur together.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
(a) Conversion (an enzymatic or TAPS-type method), because only conversion gives a fraction at one
base and these methods tolerate low input. (b) Antibody enrichment, because the question is where,
at region resolution, and it needs no conversion. (c) Native long reads, because only a single
molecule read through carries the relation between sites; short converted reads lose it.
:::

# Self-check

1. Why does a methyl group not show up in a copy by a polymerase?
2. What does the unmethylated spike-in measure, and what does the methylated one?
3. Which cytosine reads as C in oxBS-seq? In TAB-seq? In TAPS?
4. What does the 5' end of an iCLIP read mark?
5. Why do native readouts keep information that conversion loses?
6. What is the arithmetic that makes reduced representation cheaper?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. The polymerase pairs the base, and a methyl group on C does not change which base pairs with it.
2. The unmethylated one gives the failure rate of conversion; the methylated one shows whether
   the real signal survived.
3. 5mC in oxBS-seq; 5hmC in TAB-seq; unmodified C in TAPS.
4. The nucleotide next to the crosslink: reverse transcriptase stops there.
5. They read the original molecule, and many sites on it, rather than a converted copy.
6. Genome size × fraction covered × depth, with the fraction small.
:::
